To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
FIN 48 caused significant restatements, but did not cause a significant increase in the level of earnings management.
FIN 48 caused a significant increase in variability in the effective tax rates for US firms, but IFRS will not have the same effect on US firms.

1) FIN 48 has significantly changed accounting for income taxes; 2) FIN 48 appears not to be associated with earnings management; 3) FIN 48 is associated with a significant increase in effective tax rates in the year of adoption; and 4) FIN 48 may be associated with an increase in effective tax rate variability in the year of implementation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accounting for income taxes and the impact of the recent and forthcoming accounting changes on financial reporting.
how the accounting for income taxes is affected by changes in accounting standards, and what the implications of those changes are for financial reporting.
the effects of accounting standards on earnings management, earnings quality and tax avoidance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FIN 48 and the adoption of IFRS are likely to have a significant and long lasting effect on the reporting of financial statements, and the reporting of income taxes in particular.
, although the adoption of FIN 48 did not cause an increase in the level of tax avoidance, the variability in effective tax rate increased.
FIN 48 is an accounting rule that is likely to have significant effects on earnings management and effective tax rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FIN 48 is here to stay, and IFRS adoption will be a significant change in US accounting for income taxes.
the accounting for taxes will continue to be a source of volatility in financial reporting, but the volatility is likely to be reduced over time as the new standards are better understood.
FIN 48 has caused disruption in reporting standards for income tax, but has not caused a significant change in earnings management.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the accounting for income taxes is a moving target, and the accounting profession and regulators must be vigilant in ensuring that accounting for income taxes does not become a tool for managing earnings.
FIN 48 and IFRS are not likely to have a large effect on the overall level of earnings management.
accounting for income taxes will continue to evolve and will be a source of significant volatility in earnings and effective tax rates.
